Taxable savings: a higher dollar balance does not always mean more purchasing power

Follow gross interest through a simplified annual tax payment, calculate the exact real rate and separate nominal cash reconciliation from purchasing-power adjustments.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore interest retained after a simplified annual tax payment

Interactive planning lab

Nominal annual rate retained after the assumed tax2.40%
Annual change in purchasing power after tax and inflation-0.58%
Gross annual rate required just to preserve purchasing power5.00%

Original constant-rate example of fully taxable interest on accessible savings. At each year-end, interest is credited, the assumed combined tax rate applies to that interest, and that tax is paid immediately from the same savings balance. Only net interest stays invested. This timing is an arithmetic convention, not tax withholding, a filing deadline or a CRA instalment schedule. There are no new deposits, withdrawals other than the modeled tax, fees, tax credits, loss offsets, benefit interactions or changes in tax brackets. The tax rate is a user-selected assumption, not a calculated Canadian personal tax rate. The inflation input is a constant assumption, not current CPI. Real values are expressed in the purchasing power of the starting date. The before-tax reference is a mathematical comparison, not a registered-account recommendation or promise of a market yield.

  3. State where the tax money comes from and when it leaves

The central idea

Compare the interest retained after tax with price growth. Keep tax-payment timing and inflation adjustments separate before interpreting an account’s growth.

01

Start with the interest that stays in the account

A hypothetical CAD 50,000 accessible savings balance earns 4% gross interest during its first year. That is CAD 2,000 before tax. With an independently assumed 40% combined tax rate on each dollar of interest, the model pays CAD 800 of tax from the same account and retains CAD 1,200.

The ending balance is CAD 51,200. Its nominal increase is 2.4%, rather than the 4% gross rate. The tax assumption is deliberately simple: it does not calculate federal or provincial brackets, credits, deductions or benefit reductions for a particular household.

The CRA’s interest-income guidance explains reporting interest paid or credited on bank accounts, including income for which no information slip is received. The source supplies reporting context; the calculator’s rate and payment timing remain original assumptions.

02

Divide by price growth to measure purchasing power

Under a constant 3% inflation assumption, an amount that bought CAD 50,000 of goods at the start would require CAD 51,500 after one year. The modeled CAD 51,200 balance is higher in dollars but falls short of that purchasing-power benchmark.

The exact annual real rate is one plus the after-tax nominal rate, divided by one plus inflation, minus one. Here that is 1.024 divided by 1.03, minus one: approximately negative 0.58%. Simply subtracting 3% from 2.4% gives a nearby approximation, rather than the exact compound relationship.

The Bank of Canada’s investment calculator also distinguishes interest and inflation effects when illustrating savings values. This article uses its own model and inputs. Neither the 4% interest assumption nor 3% inflation is a current market observation, a product quote or a forecast.

03

State where the tax money comes from and when it leaves

Every modeled year credits interest to the opening balance, then pays tax immediately from that balance. The next year earns interest only on what remains. This convention makes the compounding effect of retained net interest inspectable.

Real tax payments follow the applicable reporting and payment requirements. A bank does not necessarily withhold the assumed amount merely because this example subtracts tax at year-end. A household paying tax from employment income would also need to record that outside cash contribution before comparing total household resources.

Keep this accessible-savings example separate from a locked investment whose interest is taxable before cash can be withdrawn. The CRA page discusses term deposits and similar investments separately. Use confirmed account terms and actual tax dates when building a funding calendar; the related instalment guide explains why reserving money and paying tax are different events.

04

Compare nominal growth with the same amount of starting-date buying power

The line chart shows three labelled paths: a before-tax reference balance, the balance after the modeled annual tax payments, and that after-tax balance expressed in starting-date purchasing power. No path receives new deposits or spending withdrawals.

The before-tax reference leaves every gross interest dollar invested. It is a mathematical reference, not an assertion that a registered account is available, appropriate or able to provide the assumed rate. Its extra ending value includes the compounding effect of interest that the taxed account could no longer retain.

The real path divides the after-tax balance by the cumulative price-growth factor. Inflation is not a separate invoice deducted from the account. A gap between nominal and real values is a difference in valuation units. Compare the real path with the original principal when asking whether buying power has increased.

05

Reconcile the actual interest ledger before attributing the gap

The waterfall begins with initial cash, adds the gross interest actually earned by the taxed account and subtracts the modeled tax actually paid from it. Those steps reconcile exactly to its ending nominal balance.

Use that account’s own annual interest amounts. Subtracting its tax from the untouched reference account’s much larger interest total would combine two different balance paths. The tax also changes later interest, so the ending-value difference between paths is not generally equal to the simple sum of tax payments.

The chart excludes fees and all personal tax interactions. Its interest and tax totals are cash-model components, not a completed tax return or an amount to copy onto a reporting slip. Reconcile real income to the actual statements and applicable tax guidance before filing.

06

A required break-even rate is a threshold, not an available offer

With the model’s assumptions, preserving buying power requires gross interest times one minus the assumed tax rate to equal inflation. At 40% tax and 3% inflation, that implies a 5% gross annual rate. The threshold covers no fee, withdrawal or other cost.

The matrix varies the tax and inflation assumptions while retaining the selected gross interest rate. Its cells are annual real rates; principal and the number of years do not change that annual relationship. Those controls do change how many dollars the balance path gains or loses over time.

Do not turn the required rate into a reason to accept a product’s risk or restrictions. The household may need accessible cash for near-term payments even when its modeled real return is negative. This example clarifies the trade-off and the cash assumptions without selecting an account, recommending an investment or promising a return.
